answer.summary: “Additional information” means task-relevant background supplied to help the model understand the situation and do the task better—not a special prompt technique. Examples include personal or work history for drafting an email, company background for data analysis, or research explaining a concept the model doesn’t know. Schulhoff often puts it at the beginning; how much to include depends partly on cost and latency in product settings.

sections.heading: Meaning and examples
sections.content: Schulhoff uses “additional information” for relevant information about the task or situation that gives the model better perspective. For email writing, that might be your work history and biography; for company-data analysis, a profile of the company. In a research example, he supplied material explaining “entrapment,” a concept the model did not know, and found that removing or anonymizing the professor’s email was followed by a sharp performance drop—an illustration of how important such information can be, though he described prompting effects as unpredictable.

sections.heading: How to include it
sections.content: He says he often puts this information at the beginning: repeated calls with the same initial context may be cheaper through caching, and putting a very long block at the end can cause the model to lose track of the original task or latch onto a question in that material. In conversational use, he is generally willing to include a lot; in product-focused settings, cost and latency make it more important to select what is needed. He usually adds the information without XML or other structured formatting, though he says formatting is optional if it suits the prompt.

sections.heading: How it fits into a prompt
sections.content: He distinguishes additional information from prompting techniques: it is a component of a prompt, alongside the role, examples, directive (the core intent), and output formatting. A technique, by his definition, is a special prompt structure or phrase intended to improve performance.

answer.summary: Schulhoff means supplying task-relevant background that helps the model understand what it is being asked to do—not just the instruction itself.

sections.heading: What counts as additional information
sections.content: He uses the phrase instead of “context,” which he considers overloaded. The idea is to give the model as much information about the task as may help it respond well. For an email, that could include your work history or biography; for company data analysis, it could be a profile of the company to help the model judge what analysis is useful and relevant.

sections.heading: Illustration and nuance
sections.content: In a research task classifying posts for “entrapment,” Schulhoff supplied research explaining the concept and an email describing the problem. Removing or anonymizing the email sharply reduced performance, illustrating how seemingly small pieces of task background can matter unpredictably. He treats good additional information as a component of a prompt, not a prompting technique in itself.
